Flout

FLOWT (rhymes with shout) · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To flout to openly disobey or disregard (a rule, law, or convention).

The restaurant continued to flout the city's health code violations even after three separate warnings.

Worked Example

Rather than quietly bending the dress code, the new employee showed up in bright sneakers and a graphic T-shirt on his very first day, flouting the company's policy in front of the entire office.

He didn't just forget the rule -- he broke it openly and on purpose, in a way everyone could see. That visible, deliberate defiance is exactly what flout describes.

How Flout Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

defy

defy: to boldly resist or refuse to obey

disregard

disregard: to pay no attention to; to ignore

Antonyms

comply

comply: to act in accordance with a rule or request

observe

observe: to follow or obey a law or custom

How Strong Is It? — overlook → flout → defy

overlook vs. flout

overlook vs. flout: To overlook a rule can be an accident or a small oversight, much less deliberate than flouting it.

defy vs. flout

defy vs. flout: To defy authority outright is an even more direct, confrontational challenge than simply flouting a rule.

Put it together

Put it together: The exact origin of flout is disputed -- some trace it to an old word meaning to mock or deride, but no single confirmed root survives into other common English words today.

Use the root in a new word: flout (origin note)

Use the root in a new word: flout (origin note): Word historians still disagree about exactly where flout came from, which is part of why it has no clear family of related English words today.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Flout is nearly always about rules, laws, or conventions -- and it always implies the person knew the rule and broke it anyway, out in the open, rather than by accident. Compare it with impinge, which usually describes a more gradual, sometimes unintentional intrusion rather than open, deliberate defiance.
